pages.text:
*From the Walk-Book of Highstep, Day 6. Weather: clear, cold. Distance: three miles. Direction: left, and confident. Mo is missing from supper. Again.*

The rain had stopped, leaving the Ridge slick and smelling of wet pine resin. Mo pulled his green poncho tighter against the chill. The ridge was a long, grey band of rock that ran down the center of Tor’s back, slick with moss that clung to the stone like a stubborn sock. He walked slowly, careful of his bare feet.

Behind him, Admiral the goat trotted with a tin bell that clinked in time with Mo’s steps. The goat had not asked to come. He had simply decided that if Mo was going to climb the mountain, so was he. It was a very logical plan, in goat terms.

Far below, the lights of Highstep twinkled in the dark. They looked like a spilled jar of sugar, tiny and sweet and scattered across the dark green blanket of the forest. Mo paused, pressing one heel firmly into the cold rock. He waited. The mountain breathed, a slow, deep exhale that ruffled the tips of the pines.

He looked up. The ridge disappeared into the shadow of the pines, leading toward the head of the mountain. The air was cold and smelled of old wood and stone.
pages.image: A small boy in a green poncho walks barefoot on a mossy rock ridge at night, followed by a large brown and white goat with a tin bell, while tiny village lights glow below in the dark forest.

pages.text:
The head of the mountain was a place of deep shadows and old roots. The pines here were ancient, their branches heavy with needles that dropped like soft, green snow. Among them, Tor’s great ear lifted out of the trees. It was not quite an ear, not really, but a curve of stone and skin that folded back on itself like a cupped hand.

Mo climbed over a low wall of roots and found the cave. It was a hollow in the rock, warm and dry. A single lantern burned on a shelf, casting a circle of orange light against the dark stone.

Old Hale sat on a wooden stool in the center of the light. He was lean, with a beard that looked like a snowdrift that had decided to stay on his chin. He wore a knitted cap with earflaps that hung down to his shoulders. His eyes were closed. He was humming.

It was a low sound, a vibration that Mo felt in his chest before he heard it with his ears. Hale hummed back at the mountain. It was a conversation, one-sided and gentle.

"Evening," said Mo, stopping at the edge of the light.

Hale did not open his eyes. He did not stop humming.
pages.image: An old man with a wild white beard and a knitted cap with earflaps sits on a stool in a stone cave, humming, while a lantern casts warm light on a small boy standing in the shadows.

pages.text:
"You fidget," said Hale. His voice was dry, like leaves skittering on stone. "I can hear it in your toes."

Mo stood very still, refusing to blink even though his eyes burned, and waited for the hum to finish, but it went on and on, a long winding melody that seemed to have no end. Admiral, the goat, had found a flat rock and lay down with his head on his paws, and the tin bell stopped clinking.

Mo’s legs ached, and his poncho itched, and he wanted to ask why, what, and where, but he kept his mouth shut. He listened to the hum, and he felt it change. It was not the walking hum, the steady roll of the Long Walk. It was softer. Rounder.

After a long time, the humming stopped. The silence settled in, smelling of woodsmoke and old stone.

"Better," said Hale.

Mo exhaled, and his knees felt like water.
pages.image: A boy in a green poncho stands perfectly still in a cave while a large goat sleeps on the floor nearby, listening to an unseen sound in the quiet, lantern-lit space.

pages.text:
Hale opened one eye, bright and sharp, and looked at Mo with an intensity that made the boy want to stand up straighter. "The song has changed," he said.

Mo nodded. He had felt the shift in the soles of his feet, a subtle difference from the usual steady rhythm. The mountain was not just walking; she was pausing, testing the ground before each foot landed.

"For fifty years," Hale said, leaning back on his stool and resting his knitted cap on his knee, "it was a walking song. Forward, forward, and around. Steady as a heartbeat." He tapped his finger once on his shin. "But this spring, it is slow. Rounder. And there is a long, low note at the end of each line, the way you hold the last crumb of a scone you really like."

Mo looked at the stone wall, watching a patch of moss sway gently in the breeze. "What does it mean?"

Hale smiled, a small and sad expression that crinkled the corners of his eyes. "It sounds," he said, "like a song about going home."

Mo felt a little jump in his chest. Home. They were home. They were on the mountain, in Highstep, with the cheese caves and the rope bridges. That was home. But the word felt different in Hale’s mouth. It felt like a place that was very far away, and very close, at the same time.

"Whose home?" Mo asked.

Hale looked at him, and his smile faded into the shadows of the cave.
pages.image: An old man with a white beard sits in a cave, looking at a young boy with a serious expression, while a lantern flickers in the background, creating a warm, intimate atmosphere.

pages.text:
"That," said Hale, "is the question, isn't it?"

He closed his eye again. The lantern flame wavered, casting long, dancing shadows against the rock walls.

"I will say no more tonight," Hale said. "Some things you have to hear for yourself. You have to feel the ground under your own feet, Mo. Not mine."

Mo stood up. His legs were stiff, but he felt lighter, somehow. As if a weight he had not known he was carrying had been set down.

He walked to the entrance of the cave. The night air was cold and crisp. Far below, in the valley of the village, a very small bell rang. It was a quick, anxious sound. Someone in Highstep had started to pack.

Mo looked down at the lights. They seemed smaller now. Dimmer. He turned back to the dark ridge, and began to climb.
pages.image: A small boy in a green poncho stands at the entrance of a cave, looking down at distant village lights, while an old man sits in the background, listening to the night.
